newsitem.title: UK: Key UK constituencies in Thursday's election.
newsitem.headline: Key UK constituencies in Thursday's election.

text.p: Voting will take place in 659 constituencies in Britain's election on Thursday, but only a handful will have a real impact on the result because of the country's first past-the-post electoral system.
Following are a list of constituencies where the result will give a clear indication of how the country is voting and whether the Labour Party can end 18 years of Conservative rule -

1. BASILDON - Achieved mythical status at 1992 election when Conservatives held on to seat, giving early indication ruling party was heading for shock win. Labour needs a 2.2 percent swing to win this time and it is number 22 on Labour's target list of marginals.

2. BIRMINGHAM EDGBASTON - Held by Conservatives and seen as key indicator seat. Like Basildon in 1992, it will declare its result early and a Labour win would be a clear indication the party was heading for power. Labour needs a 5.0 percent swing which if achieved nationwide would give it 10-15 seat majority.

3. GRAVESHAM - Electors in this seat south-east of London has voted for the party that won the election in every contest since 1951. In 1992 the Conservatives won by 5,493 votes. Labour needs a swing of 4.6 percent to win, just above the national swing of 4.3 percent needed for overall victory.

4. STIRLING - Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth is defending a wafer-thin 236-vote majority after boundary changes removed the richest small town in Scotland from the constituency. He is the most likely cabinet minister to lose his seat. Nationalist strength in fringe areas could the vote of second-placed Labour.

5. EDINBURGH PENTLANDS - Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind has held Edinburgh Pentlands for 23 years but would be unseated by a 4.5 percent swing to Labour. Pentlands is often called the most socially divided constituency in Britain. A 30 percent vote for Liberal Democrats and SNP in 1992 could work against Labour.

6. INVERNESS - Stretches from Nairn on the Moray Firth in the east to the small islands of Eigg, Muck, Canna and Rum off the west coast. It is the only four-way marginal in Britain. The seat was held by Liberal Democrat Sir Russell Johnston since 1964. He won by 458 votes over Labour in 1992, but has retired.

7. ST IVES - Anger at Europe and Conservatives over fish and beef issues make this a bellwether constituency in south-west of England which increasingly turning Liberal Democrat. Referendum Party also likely to take vital support from Conservatives. Liberals need 1.4 percent swing to unseat Conservative.

8. PUTNEY - A high-profile showdown between Sir James Goldsmith, leader of the Referendum Party, and David Mellor, Conservative minister sacked soon after 1992 election after sexual and other revelations. Labour are the main opposition party and need a swing of 7.8 percent to win.

9. TATTON - Of little importance to national result, it is a totemic constituency to many voters pitching former minister Neil Hamilton against war correspondent Martin Bell, standing as an anti-corruption independent. Bell, a former BBC reporter, is favourite to win what is the Conservatives' fifth safest seat.

10. WORCESTER - Worcester Woman, as symbol of the middle-class voter being wooed by Labour, has taken over from Essex Man as one of keys to election. Labour needs a 2.8 percent swing to win but it has never in its history elected a non-Conservative MP.

11. MID ULSTER - Rivalry among nationalist parties allowed William McCrea, an outspoken pro-British Protestant, to hold this rural 60 percent Catholic seat for the Democratic Unionist Party since 1983. Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief strategist, and the SDLP's Denis Haughey are duelling to oust McCrea, a hymn-singing politician-preacher loathed by Catholics.

12. WEST BELFAST - Gerry Adams, leader of Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political arm, is bidding to unseat Joe Hendron of the moderate Social Democratic and Labour Party and put pressure on London for a seat in peace talks. Adams held the seat from 1983 to 1992 but never took his seat in London's parliament. SDLP beat Sinn Fein by 589 votes in 1992.
